## How Do I Secure Vibe-Coded Apps Built by People Who Aren't Developers?

URL: https://arithim.com/insight-how-to-secure-vibe-coded-apps.html

Insights / Application security

# How Do I Secure Vibe-Coded Apps Built by People Who Aren't Developers?

APPSEC · RESEARCH·21 OCT 2026·6 MIN READ·BY TARUN BULCHANDANI

Treat them like any other application your company runs. Find them, give each one a named owner, scan them with the same tools you use on the rest of your code, and decide which of them are allowed near customer data. Most of these apps never pass through the systems where a security team would normally catch problems, which is why they need a process of their own.

This piece follows our look at whether you need more than one application security testing tool. It draws on Gartner's Hype Cycle for Secure Software Engineering, 2026 and its 2025 Magic Quadrant for Application Security Testing, plus what the tool vendors offer today.

## Why vibe-coded apps are a security problem

A finance analyst who builds an invoice tracker with an AI app builder has done something useful, but none of the usual checks happened along the way. Nobody reviewed the code, nobody scanned the open-source packages the AI chose, the database password is probably sitting in the source, and the app may be on the public internet because that was the default.

Gartner's 2026 Hype Cycle for Secure Software Engineering says this directly. Vibe-coded prototypes can reach production without security checks, coding agents can pull in vulnerable or malicious packages, and the MCP servers those agents connect to can have access nobody approved. Gartner's 2025 Magic Quadrant for Application Security Testing cites its own survey finding that 66% of organisations using AI tools in software development saw little or no improvement in code security. An independent study from Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology found that almost half of the code samples produced by five AI models contained bugs, many of them exploitable.

A developer who sees a scanner finding can usually judge whether it's serious. Someone who builds apps from a finance or operations role can't, and shouldn't have to.

## Where these apps tend to live

Common places to find them include:

repositories in personal GitHub or GitLab accounts, often created with a work email address

apps deployed straight from an AI app builder to its own hosting, on a subdomain the company doesn't control

internal tools running on a laptop or a spare cloud account outside the landing zone

low-code apps and automations connected to company SaaS through personal API tokens

MCP servers and coding-agent configurations on individual machines

None of these show up in the tools a security team normally watches, because those tools only see code that someone has put into a governed repository and pipeline.

## A practical process

### 1. Find them

Start with the signals you already have. Single sign-on and OAuth grant logs show which AI builders people have connected to company accounts. Expense and card data shows who is paying for them. DNS and certificate records show new subdomains. Your source control admin console shows repositories created outside the main organisation, and network logs show traffic to AI coding services. Several application security vendors now offer discovery of AI assets as well, which helps with code that is already in a repository.

### 2. Give each app an owner and a tier

For every app you find, record who uses it, what data it touches and who can reach it. Then place it in a tier, such as prototype, internal tool or business-critical. The tier decides how much scrutiny it gets. A prototype that only its builder uses needs a quick scan and a reminder. An app that holds customer records needs the same review as anything else that holds customer records.

### 3. Scan it like any other code

Move the code into a repository your scanners cover and run the same static analysis, dependency checks and secrets scanning you run everywhere else. For anything above prototype, also check that login actually works the way the owner thinks it does, and run a dynamic scan against the deployed app. Gartner recommends keeping traditional SAST and SCA tools alongside AI code assistants, and we agree. Some newer tools, such as Semgrep Guardian and OX Security's VibeSec, check code while an AI agent is writing it, which helps for builders whose tools support them.

### 4. Explain the findings in plain language

A finding like "SQL injection in search.py, line 42" means nothing to most app builders. "Anyone who types this into the search box can read every customer record" does. For each finding, explain what an attacker could do, and give the owner a fix they can apply. Often the most useful fix is a prompt they can paste back into the AI tool that wrote the code, followed by a rescan to confirm it worked.

### 5. Make the safe route the easy one

Gartner's advice for secure development generally is to make security the path of least resistance, and it fits here. Approve a short list of AI builders behind single sign-on. Provide templates with login, secrets handling and logging already done. Give coding agents the minimum permissions they need, which Gartner calls "least agency", and require a human review before anything high-risk goes live.

## Why a ban rarely works

Banning AI app builders is the obvious response, and it usually backfires. The people building these apps are solving real problems, and a ban moves their work onto personal accounts and credit cards where you have even less visibility. A short approved list with good templates gets you more control.

## Where an agent helps

Most of this process is repetitive coordination. Someone has to watch the discovery signals, open a record for each new app, ask the builder a few questions, run the scans, translate the results and chase the fix. We think an intake agent can do most of that. It would pick up a new app from the logs, message the builder in Slack or Teams to confirm ownership and purpose, run the scans, and write up each finding in plain language with a suggested fix. A person on the security team would still approve any move to the business-critical tier.

This is one of the agents we described in our application security research. As far as we can see, no vendor covers it end to end yet. Several discover AI assets, but finding an app is only the first step.

## Common questions

### What is vibe coding?

Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want to an AI tool in plain language and accepting the code it produces, often without reading it closely. It lets people with no development background build working apps in an afternoon.

### Are vibe-coded apps less secure than apps written by developers?

Often, yes, mainly because they skip the checks developer code goes through. Gartner's 2026 research warns that vibe-coded prototypes can reach production without any security review, and a 2024 Georgetown CSET study found that almost half of the code samples produced by five AI models contained bugs, many of them exploitable.

### Should we ban AI app builders?

We don't recommend it. A ban tends to push the work onto personal accounts and credit cards, where you can't see it at all. Approving a small set of tools, behind single sign-on, with templates that already handle login and secrets, gives people a safer route that's also the easier one.

### Which tools check AI-generated code for vulnerabilities?

Your existing SAST, SCA and secrets scanners work on AI-generated code once it's in a repository they cover. Some newer tools check code as an AI agent writes it, such as Semgrep Guardian and OX Security's VibeSec. Gartner recommends keeping traditional SAST and SCA alongside AI code assistants.

### Who should own a vibe-coded app?

The person or team that uses it should be its named business owner, responsible for keeping it patched or retiring it. Security sets the rules and runs the scans; the owner answers for what the app does with company data.

## Do You Need More Than One Application Security Testing Tool?

URL: https://arithim.com/insight-more-than-one-application-security-testing-tool.html

Insights / Application security

# Do You Need More Than One Application Security Testing Tool?

APPSEC · RESEARCH·20 OCT 2026·8 MIN READ·BY TARUN BULCHANDANI

Probably. When Gartner compared 16 application security testing vendors in October 2025, none of them covered the whole field well, and most large engineering organisations already run three or four of these tools side by side. Adding another scanner is rarely the hard decision. What tends to go wrong is the work between the tools, and that is the part we think AI agents are suited to.

We're writing a series on where agents fit alongside software that companies have already bought. This one starts from Gartner's Critical Capabilities for Application Security Testing, adds what each vendor says about its own product today, and ends with the agents we would build.

## What Gartner's 2025 comparison found

Gartner scored 16 vendors on 15 capabilities, including static and dynamic testing, software bills of materials, pipeline security and AI coding assistants. It then weighted those scores for six buyer scenarios, among them enterprise, DevSecOps, cloud-native and software supply chain security.

The core scanners now give broadly similar results. Gartner says this about SAST, DAST, IAST and SCA, and notes that price per developer has become one of the main ways buyers choose between them.

Coverage beyond the core is uneven. On Gartner's scale of 1 to 5, where 3 means a product meets requirements, the best score any vendor got in any of the six scenarios was about 3.5. Counting through the published ratings ourselves, we found interactive testing weak or missing at 12 of the 16 vendors, and pipeline security weak or missing at 7 of them, with a median score of 1.6. Dynamic testing was weak at 7 vendors and API testing at 6. Many vendors close these gaps through partners or OEM deals, which Gartner describes as fragile arrangements.

Gartner also observes that many large organisations have assembled their own application security platform out of several vendors' products, since nobody sells a complete one yet, and that teams increasingly report application risk instead of raw counts of findings.

## What each vendor is known for

Each vendor is strong somewhere different, which is why most stacks end up mixed. The table summarises Gartner's ratings from September 2025, with our note on what buyers usually add alongside each product.

VendorKnown forUsually paired with something for

ApiiroRisk graph and posture management; top score for ASPMDynamic, container and IaC testing

Black DuckBroad suite, strong IAST, ASPM that ingests third-party toolsPipeline security; lighter needs at SMB scale

CheckmarxCheckmarx One, ASPM, developer enablementIAST and mobile binary scanning

Contrast SecurityRuntime-first: IAST, RASP, detection and responsePipeline, container and IaC coverage

CycodePipeline and supply chain security; first for SSCSDAST, API and IAST

Data TheoremCloud-native, API, container and mobile testingPipeline and artifact integrity

GitHubAdvanced Security in the developer workflow; supply chainDAST, IAST, API, IaC and containers; AI features need GitHub.com

GitLabOne DevSecOps platform with end-to-end pipeline visibilityDeeper DAST, IAST and AI risk

HCLSoftwareAppScan full suite; first for the enterprise scenarioAPI business-logic testing; supply chain via a partner

JFrogSoftware supply chain, SCA and runtime contextDynamic and API testing

Mend.ioComposition analysis and automated dependency updatesDAST, IAST and secrets detection

OpenTextFortify: enterprise breadth, air-gapped deployment, AI-risk detectionContainer and pipeline security

SemgrepCustom rules on source code, with open-source rootsDynamic, API and container testing; cross-tool orchestration

SnykDeveloper-first suite and AppRisk posture managementPipeline security and IAST

SonatypeComposition analysis, repository firewall, AI component detectionSAST, DAST, IaC and posture management

VeracodeSAST and SCA, pen-testing service, EU data regionPipeline security and IAST

Summarised from Gartner's ratings as of 9 September 2025. Vendors have shipped a lot since, so check current capabilities with each of them.

In practice a large organisation might run GitHub or GitLab for repository-native scanning, a deeper scanner such as Checkmarx, Veracode, Black Duck, OpenText or HCL, a supply chain tool like JFrog, Sonatype or Mend.io, and increasingly a posture management product such as Apiiro, Cycode, Snyk AppRisk or Checkmarx ASPM on top. Each of these has its own console and its own idea of severity, and their findings overlap.

## Work no single tool owns

Comparing the gaps side by side, seven jobs keep turning up that no individual product is responsible for.

### Getting a finding fixed and merged

Most vendors can now suggest an AI-generated fix. Getting that fix merged still means working out which team owns the code, getting someone to review the change, waiting for tests, checking that the next scan no longer reports the issue, and closing the ticket before its SLA runs out. Those steps cross Jira or ServiceNow, Slack or Teams, and the repository, and in most organisations an AppSec engineer still does them by hand.

### Triage across scanners

When the same vulnerability appears in two tools under different identifiers, or a finding sits in code that never runs in production, someone has to decide what to keep. Posture management products are built to correlate these findings, but plenty of organisations haven't bought one, and those that have usually still run a tool or two it doesn't ingest cleanly.

### Pipeline security

Pipeline security is the weakest capability across the vendors Gartner rated. Doing it properly starts with an inventory of CI/CD runners, stored secrets and the third-party actions and plugins each pipeline pulls in, and then checks build integrity against a framework such as SLSA. We would be surprised if most teams had even the inventory.

### Vibe-coded apps outside the pipeline

Gartner calls out vibe coding, where people with little development background use AI to build working applications, as a new attack surface, because those apps tend to sit outside normal security processes. A scanner only tests code that someone points it at, so finding these apps, giving each one an owner and getting it scanned is currently nobody's job.

### Models, prompts and MCP servers

Applications now ship with models, prompts and Model Context Protocol servers inside them, and Gartner recommends choosing tools that scan those artifacts as well. Several vendors have added this in the past year. Keeping one inventory across every repository and team, and checking it against something like the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications, is still mostly a governance task.

### Reporting risk to the board

If risk is going to be the KPI, someone has to combine findings from several tools into a trend for each application and explain why it moved. In many organisations that is still a spreadsheet assembled by hand before each quarterly review.

### Switching vendors

Gartner points out that changing AST vendors is contractually easier than it used to be, but re-instrumenting every pipeline is real work, so organisations often renew tools they have outgrown.

## Where we think agents fit

Each of those jobs involves reading from a few systems, making a judgement with some context, acting in another system and keeping a record of why. Agents handle that kind of work well, provided they use the tools a customer already has. These are the ones we would build.

A remediation agent that picks up a prioritised finding from any scanner, finds the owner from CODEOWNERS or the CMDB and drafts a fix, using the vendor's own autofix where there is one. It opens the pull request, follows up with reviewers, confirms the rescan is clean and closes the ticket. A person approves every merge.

A triage agent that deduplicates findings across tools, checks whether the vulnerable code is reachable, and records its reason for setting anything aside, so the security team can audit what it filtered out.

A pipeline auditor that inventories GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins or Azure DevOps configuration, scores it against policy and SLSA, and proposes changes as pull requests.

An intake agent for AI-built and low-code apps that finds them, gets them scanned and explains the results to owners who aren't developers.

A reporting agent that writes the monthly application risk summary for the CISO and the board from every tool at once, with its working shown.

A migration agent that maps rules and policies from one scanner to another, rewrites pipeline configuration and runs both tools in parallel until their results line up. Some vendors run switching programmes of their own, but those only move customers toward that vendor.

## What vendors are shipping in 2026

The vendors have moved a long way since Gartner's ratings. Apiiro and Cycode now market themselves as platforms for securing agentic development. Many vendors publish MCP servers so coding assistants can read their findings, and several now check AI-written code as it is generated, Semgrep Guardian being one example. GitHub's Copilot Autofix proposes fixes for code scanning alerts on pull requests and on the default branch.

This makes an agent layer easier to build, because there are better interfaces to call. Each vendor's AI still only sees that vendor's findings, though, and most of the new features target code being written today. The backlog already sitting in four consoles gets less attention. We expect the gaps between products to stay open for a while.

## How we would start

We would begin by mapping the tools you have, what their APIs expose and where findings tend to stall. Then we would pick the loop that costs your team the most time, usually remediation or triage, and put one agent into production on it, with approvals and an audit trail from the first day. If time to remediate, SLA breaches or the amount of noise rejected improves, we extend it. If it doesn't, we stop there.

## Common questions

### Do we need more than one application security testing tool?

For most large organisations, yes. In Gartner's 2025 assessment no vendor scored much above 3.5 out of 5 in any buyer scenario, and most rely on partners for at least one capability. It is worth deciding early how the tools will share findings and who owns the result.

### Our AppSec vendor already has AI autofix. What would an agent add?

Autofix writes a patch for a finding inside one product. Most of the time to remediate goes on finding the owner, getting a review, verifying the fix with a rescan and updating tickets across several products, and an agent can take on that surrounding work.

### Is an agent layer the same as buying an ASPM product?

Posture management gives you a single prioritised view across tools. An agent acts on that view by opening pull requests, chasing reviews and closing tickets. You can use both, and an agent can deliver some of the value before an ASPM product is in place.

### How do I secure apps that people vibe-coded with AI?

Find them first by looking for new repositories, low-code projects and deployed apps that none of your scanners cover. Give each one a named owner, run it through the same SAST, SCA and secrets scanning as the rest of your code, and explain the findings in plain language, because the person who built it may not be a developer.

### How do you keep AI agents safe inside a security workflow?

Give each agent least-privilege credentials for each tool, require human approval for every change, log every decision with its reasoning, and treat model output as untrusted input.

## Operational Intelligence vs Automation

URL: https://arithim.com/insight-operational-intelligence-vs-automation.html

Insights / Operational intelligence

# Operational Intelligence vs Automation

OPERATIONAL INTELLIGENCE·18 JAN 2026·2 MIN READ·BY TARUN BULCHANDANI

Automation moves a task from manual execution to structured execution. Operational intelligence improves how information, judgement, and action move through a business.

Both matter. But they solve different problems, and confusing the two is how AI projects end up impressive in a demo and useless in production.

Automation is useful when a repeatable step can be handled consistently: the same input, the same rule, the same result, every time. Operational intelligence is useful when teams need visibility, context, evidence, or decision support across a changing environment, where the "right" action depends on what else is true at that moment.

Automation for dependable execution. Intelligence for coordination and control.

Strong systems usually contain both. The discipline is knowing which one a given problem actually needs, and not paying for the wrong one.

Insights / AI implementation

# What Most Businesses Actually Need From AI

AI IMPLEMENTATION·08 JAN 2026·2 MIN READ·BY TARUN BULCHANDANI

Most organisations do not need a louder AI strategy. They need a clearer operating model for where AI can reduce friction, improve coordination, and support better decisions.

Useful AI work usually starts with ordinary questions: where does information stall, where do teams repeat low-value work, where does reporting arrive too late, and where does knowledge live outside the systems people use every day.

The implementation path is often smaller and more disciplined than the hype suggests. Map the workflow, identify the decision points, improve the data surface, then introduce automation or intelligence where it genuinely changes the work.

AI becomes valuable when it is part of a system people can trust, operate, and improve.

That is the whole game. Not the model, not the demo, but the system around it that survives a normal Tuesday.

Our interests are not abstract AI capability in isolation, but the systems required to make intelligence useful inside real operational environments.

CURRENT THEMES

### Workflow orchestration

How intelligence and automation coordinate across the steps of real work, not just single tasks.

Structuring knowledge so humans, search engines, and AI systems read it the same way.

### Sustainability systems

Operational and reporting infrastructure for environmental and resource accountability.

### Governance-aware automation

Automation that carries its own audit trail, controls, and accountability by design.

### Operational decision support

Giving teams the visibility, context, and evidence they need to make good decisions across a changing environment.

## Privacy policy

URL: https://arithim.com/privacy.html

PRIVACY

# Privacy policy

LAST UPDATED · 21 OCTOBER 2026

## Who we are

Arithim Ltd is an applied AI company based in London, United Kingdom. It builds software products and works with clients on AI projects. This policy explains what limited information we collect through this website and how we handle it.

## What we collect

We only collect the information you choose to send us: the details you enter in the contact form, and any messages you send to hello@arithim.com or research@arithim.com. The site itself uses no advertising trackers. The contact and demo request forms use Cloudflare Turnstile to block automated submissions and Resend to deliver your message to our inbox.

## How we use it

We use your details only to respond to your enquiry and, where relevant, to discuss a potential engagement or research collaboration. We do not sell or share your information with third parties for marketing.

## Calls and chats with our AI assistants

The Call us button on this site lets you speak or type to Arithim's AI assistants. They are AI, not people, and you are told so before the call starts. The service is for people aged 18 or over, and for business enquiries. Please do not use it to share sensitive personal information such as health details. The assistants do not make any decision about you that has a legal or similarly significant effect. They answer questions, take messages and pass them to a person, who replies within one working day.

## What we collect from calls and chats

Your voice is processed live so that it can be turned into text. We ask the voice provider not to keep the audio. We keep the transcript of the conversation, the details you choose to give (such as your name, organisation, email address or phone number, and what you want to talk about), a short summary, and technical data such as your IP address, which we store only as a salted hash and use to prevent abuse and limit repeated use.

## Why we use it

We use this information to answer your enquiry, to pass your message to Tarun, to keep the service secure and within its usage limits, and to improve how the assistants answer. Our lawful basis is legitimate interests in answering enquiries and running the service safely. Where you ask us to take steps towards an engagement, we also use it to do so at your request.

## Who processes it for us

ElevenLabs processes your voice and runs the voice conversation. Anthropic provides the AI model that writes the assistants' replies. Cloudflare hosts this site and stores the call records. Resend sends the internal notification email to us. Each acts as a processor on our instructions, under its data processing terms. We do not sell this information and do not use it for marketing.

## Where your data is processed

These providers process data in the United States. Where data leaves the UK, we rely on the UK International Data Transfer Addendum, or on the UK extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, as set out in each provider's data processing terms.

## How long we keep it

ElevenLabs keeps conversation data for no more than 30 days and does not store the audio. Our own records of calls and chats are deleted after 90 days. We keep a message for longer only where it becomes an ongoing enquiry or engagement, and then under the same terms as the rest of our correspondence with you.

## Your rights

You can ask us at any time to access, correct, or delete the information you have shared with us. This includes anything you told our AI assistants. You can also object to our use of your information, ask us to restrict it, or complain to the Information Commissioner's Office. To make a request, email hello@arithim.com, quoting the reference the assistant gave you if you have one, and we will respond promptly.

## Contact

Questions about this policy can be sent to hello@arithim.com.

Call us
